lecture-02.title: Network Packets & Layered Communication Quiz
lecture-02.description: 20 questions covering OSI 7 layers, TCP/IP, Ethernet framing, MTU, PMTUD, CSMA/CD physics, and MAC addressing.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of protocol layering in computer networks?

options.text: To increase raw transmission bandwidth by striping bits across layers
To enforce separation of concerns, modularity, and independent protocol evolution
To eliminate the need for physical network interface cards
To encrypt all data packets by default across the network

questions.explanation: Layering enforces separation of concerns: each layer handles a specific task (e.g. HTTP for web documents, IP for global routing) and interacts through standardized interfaces, allowing independent upgrades.

questions.question: In the standard 7-layer OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end reliability, port multiplexing, and flow control?

options.text: Layer 2 — Data Link Layer
Layer 3 — Network Layer
Layer 4 — Transport Layer
Layer 5 — Session Layer

questions.explanation: Layer 4 (Transport Layer) delivers segments between processes using port numbers (e.g. TCP/UDP) and manages end-to-end flow control and retransmissions.

questions.question: Which of the following layers from the 7-layer OSI model are combined into the single 'Application Layer' in the 4-layer TCP/IP model? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Presentation Layer (Layer 6)
Session Layer (Layer 5)
Transport Layer (Layer 4)
Application Layer (Layer 7)

questions.explanation: The pragmatic TCP/IP model merges the OSI Application, Presentation, and Session layers into a single Application layer, handling protocols like HTTP, TLS, DNS, and SSH.

questions.question: What is the correct terminology for the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at Layer 2, Layer 3, and Layer 4 respectively?

options.text: Packet, Frame, Segment
Frame, Packet, Segment
Segment, Packet, Frame
Datagram, Frame, Packet

questions.explanation: The standardized PDU names are: Layer 2 = Frame (Ethernet/Wi-Fi), Layer 3 = Packet (IP), and Layer 4 = Segment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP).

questions.question: Why is the minimum payload for a standard Ethernet II frame set to 46 bytes (total minimum frame 64 bytes)?

options.text: To fit the 20-byte IPv4 header and 20-byte TCP header with 6 bytes of data
To ensure collision detection under CSMA/CD over the maximum network cable diameter (slot time)
Because CRC-32 requires at least 46 bytes to calculate a polynomial remainder
To prevent optical signal dispersion over fiber optic cables

questions.explanation: In half-duplex CSMA/CD networks, the transmitter must still be sending when a collision signal returns from the farthest point of the wire (slot time = 51.2 μs = 512 bits = 64 bytes).

questions.question: If an application generates a 28-byte ARP packet to be transmitted over Ethernet, what does the Data Link Layer do to meet the 64-byte frame requirement?

options.text: It fragments the ARP packet into two separate frames
It pads the frame with 18 bytes of zeroes (0x00)
It rejects the packet and sends an ICMP error
It compresses the Ethernet header

questions.explanation: The minimum payload is 46 bytes. If the payload is 28 bytes, 18 padding bytes (0x00) are appended before computing the FCS.

questions.question: Which field in the Ethernet II frame specifies the encapsulated Layer 3 protocol (e.g., 0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6)?

options.text: Preamble
Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD)
EtherType
Frame Check Sequence (FCS)

questions.explanation: EtherType is a 2-byte field indicating the multiplexed upper-layer protocol (0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6, 0x0806 for ARP).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 7-byte Preamble and 1-byte SFD (Start of Frame Delimiter) in an Ethernet transmission?

options.text: To encode encryption keys for TLS
To synchronize the physical receiver's bit clock before frame data arrives
To establish TCP sequence numbers
To store the sender's default gateway IP

questions.explanation: The alternating 10101010 pattern allows physical clock recovery circuits in the receiving NIC to lock onto the bit frequency.

questions.question: A MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes). How is it divided between the manufacturer and the device ID?

options.text: First 16 bits: Country; Last 32 bits: Device
First 24 bits: OUI (Manufacturer); Last 24 bits: Device Identifier
First 32 bits: Subnet; Last 16 bits: Host
First 8 bits: Class; Last 40 bits: Random

questions.explanation: The first 3 bytes (24 bits) form the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) assigned by IEEE to the hardware manufacturer.

questions.question: In a 48-bit MAC address, how can you determine if the address is a Unicast or Multicast address?

options.text: Inspect the least significant bit (b0) of the first byte: 0 = Unicast, 1 = Multicast
Check if the last byte is equal to 255 (0xFF)
Unicast MAC addresses always begin with 00:00:00
Check the most significant bit of the last byte

questions.explanation: Bit 0 of byte 1 is the Individual/Group (I/G) bit: 0 indicates individual (unicast), while 1 indicates group (multicast).

questions.question: As an HTTP GET request travels from a client laptop to a remote web server across 4 router hops, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: The Destination MAC address changes at every router hop
The Source IP address changes at every router hop (without NAT)
The Destination IP address remains unchanged from source to server (without NAT)
The Ethernet frame is completely decapsulated and rebuilt with new MACs at each router

questions.explanation: Layer 2 frames are hop-by-hop local and rebuilt at every router. Layer 3 IP headers remain intact end-to-end across the route unless modified by NAT.

questions.question: What is standard Ethernet MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)?

options.text: 512 bytes
1024 bytes
1500 bytes
9000 bytes

questions.explanation: Standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes, which represents the maximum Layer 3 IP packet size that can be carried in an Ethernet frame.

questions.question: Given an MTU of 1500 bytes, a standard 20-byte IPv4 header, and a standard 20-byte TCP header, what is the default TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS)?

options.text: 1500 bytes
1460 bytes
1440 bytes
1480 bytes

questions.explanation: MSS = MTU - (IP Header + TCP Header) = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes.

questions.question: In IPv4 packet fragmentation, the Fragment Offset field is measured in units of:

options.text: 1 byte
4 bytes (32 bits)
8 bytes (64 bits)
16 bytes (128 bits)

questions.explanation: Because the Fragment Offset field is 13 bits long, it cannot represent individual byte positions for 65535 bytes directly; it scales by 8-byte (64-bit) blocks.

questions.question: Where are IP fragments reassembled when traveling across an internetwork?

options.text: At each intermediate router before forwarding
At the default gateway router
Strictly at the final destination host
At the first autonomous system boundary router

questions.explanation: Intermediate routers only fragment packets; they never reassemble them. Reassembly occurs exclusively at the final receiving host.

questions.question: What happens when an IP packet with the DF (Don't Fragment) bit set to 1 arrives at a router whose outgoing interface MTU is smaller than the packet size?

options.text: The router fragments the packet anyway and ignores the flag
The router compresses the packet with gzip
The router drops the packet and replies with an ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' error
The router routes the packet through loopback

questions.explanation: The router drops the packet and sends an ICMP Type 3 Code 4 message ('Fragmentation Needed and DF Set') containing its interface MTU, enabling Path MTU Discovery.

questions.question: Which of the following commands can be used on modern operating systems to view the physical MAC address of network interfaces? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: ip link show (Linux)
ipconfig /all (Windows)
ifconfig (macOS / BSD)
ping -m (Cross-platform)

questions.explanation: 'ip link show', 'ipconfig /all', and 'ifconfig' display MAC addresses. Ping is an ICMP connectivity tool, not an interface inspection tool.

questions.question: What is the broadcast MAC address used in Ethernet to send a frame to all stations on a local network segment?

options.text: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF

questions.explanation: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (all 48 bits set to 1) is the Layer 2 Ethernet broadcast address.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 4-byte Frame Check Sequence (FCS) located at the end of an Ethernet frame?

options.text: To encrypt payload data using AES-GCM
To detect transmission bit errors using a CRC-32 polynomial
To store the sender's TCP sequence number
To specify the time-to-live of the frame

questions.explanation: FCS contains a 32-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC-32). If bits are corrupted during transmission, the receiver silently drops the frame.

questions.question: Why is IP fragmentation considered harmful in modern high-performance networks? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: If any single fragment is dropped, the entire segment must be retransmitted
Intermediate fragments lack Layer 4 port headers, complicating stateful firewalls and NAT
Reassembly consumes router switching fabric memory and CPU cycles
Fragments are vulnerable to teardown and overlap security attacks

questions.explanation: A, B, and D are well-documented flaws (RFC 8900). C is incorrect because intermediate routers do not reassemble fragments; only the destination host does.

lecture-03.title: IP Addresses & Subnetting I Quiz
lecture-03.description: 20 questions covering binary conversions, CIDR notation, subnet masks, bitwise ANDing, magic numbers, and RFC 1918.

questions.question: How many total bits compose an IPv4 address, and how are they conventionally represented in human-readable form?

options.text: 32 bits represented as 4 decimal octets separated by dots
48 bits represented as 6 colon-separated hexadecimal pairs
64 bits represented as 8 decimal numbers
128 bits represented as 8 hexadecimal hextets

questions.explanation: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit unsigned binary integers written in dotted-decimal notation (e.g. 192.168.1.1).

questions.question: What is the decimal equivalent of the 8-bit binary octet 11000000?
Convert the decimal value 172 into 8-bit binary:
In traditional Classful addressing, what is the default subnet mask and first-octet leading bit pattern for a Class B network?

options.text: Leading bit 0, default mask 255.0.0.0 (/8)
Leading bits 10, default mask 255.255.0.0 (/16)
Leading bits 110, default mask 255.255.255.0 (/24)
Leading bits 1110, default mask 255.255.255.255 (/32)

questions.explanation: Class B networks have first octet range 128–191 (binary starts with 10) and default mask 255.255.0.0 (/16).

questions.question: Why was the Classful addressing system abandoned in favor of CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) in 1993?

options.text: Classful networks could not transmit Ethernet frames
Rigid /8, /16, and /24 boundaries caused massive address wastage and routing table explosion
Computers could not process bitwise AND operations
It was impossible to assign private IP addresses

questions.explanation: If an organization needed 300 IP addresses, a Class C (/24, 254 hosts) was too small, forcing them to take a Class B (/16, 65,534 hosts), wasting over 65,000 addresses.

questions.question: What mathematical operation does a router's hardware silicon perform to find the Network Address from an incoming packet's Destination IP and Subnet Mask?

options.text: Bitwise XOR
Bitwise AND
Bitwise OR
Two's Complement Addition

questions.explanation: Network Address = Destination IP AND Subnet Mask. Since 1 AND 1 = 1 and any bit AND 0 = 0, the host bits are masked to 0 while preserving the network prefix.

questions.question: Given the IP address 192.168.10.157 with subnet mask 255.255.255.224 (/27), what is the Network Address?
questions.explanation: In the 4th octet, mask 255.255.255.224 (/27) has block size 256 - 224 = 32. Multiples of 32 are 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192. For IP 192.168.10.157, the largest multiple <= 157 is 128 (since 128 <= 157 < 160). Alternatively, bitwise AND of 157 (10011101_2) & 224 (11100000_2) = 128 (10000000_2). Hence, the Network Address is 192.168.10.128.

questions.question: How many total usable host addresses are available in a /26 subnet?
questions.explanation: Host bits H = 32 - 26 = 6. Total addresses = 2^6 = 64. Usable hosts = 2^6 - 2 = 62 (subtracting Network ID and Directed Broadcast).

questions.question: Using the 'Magic Number' subnetting shortcut, what is the block size for a subnet mask of 255.255.255.240 (/28)?
questions.explanation: Magic Number = 256 - interesting_octet_mask = 256 - 240 = 16.

questions.question: What is the Directed Broadcast address for the subnet 172.16.80.0/20?
questions.explanation: Mask /20 has mask 255.255.240.0 in the 3rd octet. Block size = 256 - 240 = 16. Next subnet starts at 80 + 16 = 96. Broadcast is one less: 172.16.95.255.

questions.question: Which of the following IPv4 address ranges are officially designated as Private Address Spaces by RFC 1918? (Select ALL that apply)
Is the IP address 172.32.10.5 a private or public address?

options.text: Private, because all 172.x.x.x addresses are private
Public, because the RFC 1918 Class B range ends at 172.31.255.255
Loopback address
APIPA self-assigned address

questions.explanation: The private 172 range spans strictly from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 (16 contiguous /16 blocks). 172.32.10.5 is a globally routable public IP.

questions.question: When a device on a network displays an IP address of 169.254.42.99, what does this indicate to a network engineer?

options.text: The device has connected directly to the Google DNS server
The device failed to obtain an IP lease from a DHCP server (APIPA self-assignment)
The network interface card is operating in full duplex gigabit mode
The computer is experiencing a SYN flood attack

questions.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing). If a host sends DHCP Discovers but receives no DHCP Offer, the OS assigns an address in this range.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 127.0.0.0/8 block (e.g. 127.0.0.1)?

options.text: Default route to the internet
Loopback interface for local inter-process communication without leaving the host
Carrier-Grade NAT for mobile cellular towers
Reserved for future satellite communications

questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 (localhost) loops packets directly back up the local OS networking stack without transmitting bits over physical hardware.

questions.question: What CIDR prefix length is standard for connecting two routers over a point-to-point serial or WAN fiber link with zero wasted usable host addresses?
questions.explanation: A /30 provides 4 total addresses (2 host bits): 1 Network ID, 2 Usable Host IPs (one for each router interface), and 1 Directed Broadcast, with zero wasted host addresses.

questions.question: What is the usable host range for the subnet 192.168.100.64/26?
questions.explanation: Network ID = 192.168.100.64, First Usable = 192.168.100.65. Next block starts at 128, so Broadcast = 192.168.100.127 and Last Usable = 192.168.100.126.

questions.question: How many bits are borrowed to divide a /24 network into eight equal subnets, and what is the resulting new CIDR prefix?

options.text: 2 bits borrowed -> /26
3 bits borrowed -> /27
4 bits borrowed -> /28
8 bits borrowed -> /32

questions.explanation: To create 8 subnets: 2^S >= 8 implies S = 3 bits borrowed. New prefix = 24 + 3 = /27.

questions.question: What is the dotted-decimal subnet mask corresponding to a /21 prefix?
questions.explanation: /21 means 16 bits in first two octets (255.255) + 5 bits in the 3rd octet. 11111000 in binary = 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = 248. So 255.255.248.0.

questions.question: Which of the following addresses can NEVER be legally configured on an individual computer's network interface card? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: 192.168.1.0/24 (Network Address)
192.168.1.255/24 (Directed Broadcast)
192.168.1.1/24 (First Usable Host)
255.255.255.255 (Limited Broadcast)

questions.explanation: Network Addresses (all host bits 0) and Broadcast Addresses (all host bits 1) cannot be assigned to individual hosts. 192.168.1.1 is a valid host address (commonly used for the gateway).

questions.question: A network engineer sees the IP address 100.64.1.1 on a mobile WAN interface. What special address block does this belong to?

options.text: RFC 1918 Private Enterprise
RFC 6598 Carrier-Grade NAT (Shared Address Space for ISPs)
Multicast Class D space
Public internet space owned by Microsoft

questions.explanation: 100.64.0.0/10 is reserved by RFC 6598 for Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) so telecom operators can share public IPs among mobile devices without colliding with RFC 1918.

lecture-04.title: IP Addresses & Subnetting II Quiz
lecture-04.description: 20 questions covering VLSM partition trees, IPv6 RFC 5952 compression, scopes, Default Gateways, and NAT/PAT.

questions.question: What is the primary operational advantage of Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) over Fixed Length Subnet Masking (FLSM)?

options.text: VLSM allows assigning different subnet mask lengths to different subnets, preventing IP wastage
VLSM allows switches to ignore MAC addresses
VLSM converts IPv4 addresses into IPv6 addresses automatically
VLSM eliminates the need for a default gateway

questions.explanation: FLSM forces all subnets to have identical sizes. VLSM allows custom prefix sizing per department, drastically reducing wasted host addresses.

questions.question: What is the Golden Rule of VLSM address allocation?

options.text: Allocate the smallest subnet first to conserve the beginning of the block
Always sort host requirements in strictly descending order (Largest -> Smallest) and allocate the largest blocks first
Always assign the default gateway the highest IP in the range
Never use subnet masks longer than /24

questions.explanation: Allocating small subnets first fragments the continuous binary address space, making it impossible to allocate contiguous larger power-of-two subnets later.

questions.question: You need to accommodate 100 hosts in an engineering subnet. What is the smallest valid subnet mask and block size?

options.text: /26 (64 addresses, 62 hosts)
/25 (128 addresses, 126 hosts)
/24 (256 addresses, 254 hosts)
/27 (32 addresses, 30 hosts)

questions.explanation: 2^N - 2 >= 100 implies 2^N >= 102 -> N = 7 host bits (2^7 = 128). Prefix = 32 - 7 = /25, offering 126 usable hosts.

questions.question: How many bits are in an IPv6 address, and how many hexadecimal digits represent it?

options.text: 64 bits, 16 hex digits
128 bits, 32 hex digits arranged in 8 hextets of 4 hex digits
256 bits, 64 hex digits
48 bits, 12 hex digits

questions.explanation: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as 8 groups (hextets) of 4 hexadecimal characters (8 * 16 = 128 bits).

questions.question: According to RFC 5952, how should the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 be canonically compressed?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros in each hextet are omitted (0db8 -> db8, 0370 -> 370), and the longest consecutive run of all-zero hextets is replaced with '::'.

questions.question: Why can the double-colon '::' zero-compression symbol be used ONLY ONCE in any IPv6 address?

options.text: Because RFC standards restrict it for aesthetic reasons
Because multiple double-colons create mathematical ambiguity in reconstructing how many zero hextets belong to each run
Because hardware router ASICs cannot process more than 16 zeros
Because it would conflict with IPv4 dotted decimals

questions.explanation: If '::' appeared twice (e.g. 2001::db8::1), a parser cannot determine how many zero hextets belong to the first run vs. the second run.

questions.question: What is a major architectural difference between IPv4 and IPv6 regarding one-to-all communication?

options.text: IPv6 uses larger broadcast packets
IPv6 completely eliminates Broadcast addresses; all one-to-many operations use targeted Multicast
IPv6 requires all hosts to broadcast their MAC address every 10 seconds
IPv6 disables multicast to conserve fiber spectrum

questions.explanation: IPv6 has NO broadcast. All one-to-many communications use efficient Multicast groups (e.g. ff02::1 for all nodes, ff02::2 for all routers), preventing broadcast storms.

questions.question: Which prefix identifies an IPv6 Link-Local address automatically configured on every interface?
questions.explanation: fe80::/10 is reserved for Link-Local addresses, used for single-hop neighbor discovery (NDP) and router advertisements.

questions.question: What is the IPv6 equivalent of the IPv4 loopback address 127.0.0.1?
questions.explanation: ::1 (or 0000:...:0001) is the IPv6 loopback address.

questions.question: How does a host decide whether to deliver a packet directly on the local LAN or forward it to the Default Gateway?

options.text: It checks if the destination IP is an even or odd number
It computes (Destination IP AND Host Subnet Mask) and checks if the result equals its local Network ID
It always sends all packets to the Default Gateway regardless of destination
It pings the destination MAC address

questions.explanation: If Destination IP AND Subnet Mask == Local Network ID, the destination is on the same subnet (direct ARP). Otherwise, it forwards to the gateway router's MAC.

questions.question: Which commands can be run on Windows and Linux respectively to display the configured Default Gateway? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: route print (Windows)
ip route show (Linux)
netstat -rn (macOS / Linux)
arp -d (Windows)

questions.explanation: 'route print' (Windows), 'ip route show' (Linux), and 'netstat -rn' display the kernel routing table and default gateway. 'arp -d' purges the ARP cache.

questions.question: What primary problem does Network Address Translation (NAT / NAPT) solve for home and enterprise networks?

options.text: It speeds up light transmission in fiber optic cables
It enables hundreds of private devices to share a single public IPv4 address
It automatically assigns domain names to computers
It encrypts all DNS lookups

questions.explanation: NAT maps private RFC 1918 IPs and transport port numbers to a single public IP, alleviating immediate IPv4 address depletion.

questions.question: In Port Address Translation (PAT / NAPT), how does the router distinguish returning packets destined for two different internal devices that connected to the same external server?

options.text: By the color of the Ethernet cable
By mapping unique translated public transport-layer Port Numbers in its NAT state table
By inspecting internal MAC addresses stored in the packet payload
By broadcasting the reply to all LAN hosts

questions.explanation: PAT tracks (Private IP, Private Port) <-> (Public IP, Translated Port). The unique translated port in incoming packets indexes the correct internal host.

questions.question: What is Port Forwarding (Destination NAT / DNAT) primarily used for?

options.text: Allowing internal devices to browse external websites
Allowing external internet clients to initiate connections to a server hosted inside a private NAT network
Speeding up local Wi-Fi transmission rates
Preventing ARP cache poisoning

questions.explanation: Because NAT blocks unsolicited inbound packets by default, port forwarding maps a specific external public port permanently to an internal private host:port.

questions.question: Why do peer-to-peer applications like WebRTC, Discord voice, and multiplayer games struggle when devices are behind NAT?

options.text: NAT routers drop all UDP packets
Devices behind NAT do not know their external public IP and cannot accept direct inbound connection requests without hole punching
NAT breaks TLS encryption keys
NAT changes the speed of light

questions.explanation: NAT prevents direct inbound connections. P2P protocols must use traversal frameworks (STUN/TURN/ICE) to discover external endpoints and punch holes.

questions.question: What is the specific role of a STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) server?

options.text: It relays all voice and video packets between peers
It allows a client behind NAT to discover its public IP address and NAT port mapping as seen by the outside world
It replaces the DNS root servers
It generates SSL certificates

questions.explanation: STUN acts as an external mirror: a client queries the STUN server, which responds with the client's public IP and translated port.

questions.question: When does WebRTC fall back to using a TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) server?

options.text: When the connection speed is faster than 100 Mbps
When direct peer-to-peer hole punching fails due to Symmetric NAT or restrictive firewalls
When the client uses an Ethernet cable instead of Wi-Fi
When IPv6 is disabled

questions.explanation: TURN servers act as costly media relays when direct P2P connections cannot be established through symmetric NAT or corporate firewalls.

questions.question: Given the base network 10.0.0.0/16, how many /20 subnets can be created from this block?
questions.explanation: Borrowed bits = 20 - 16 = 4 bits. Number of subnets = 2^4 = 16 subnets.

questions.question: Which of the following are inherent architectural drawbacks or limitations of NAT? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: It violates the pure end-to-end principle of the original Internet architecture
It requires the router to maintain stateful connection tables in memory
Protocols that embed IP addresses inside their application payload (e.g. FTP, SIP) require complex Application Layer Gateways (ALGs)
It increases the size of the physical Ethernet frame beyond 1518 bytes

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are major drawbacks of NAT (RFC 2993). NAT does not increase the physical Ethernet frame size.

questions.question: What protocol replaces ARP in IPv6 networks for resolving Layer 3 IPv6 addresses to Layer 2 MAC addresses?

options.text: DHCPv6
Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP / ICMPv6)
BGP-4
Reverse ARP (RARP)

questions.explanation: IPv6 replaces broadcast ARP with Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP), utilizing ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement multicast messages.

lecture-05.title: Graph Algorithms for Networking I Quiz
lecture-05.description: 20 questions covering graph network modeling, BFS hop-count, DFS cycle detection, and Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions.question: When modeling a telecommunications network as a graph G = (V, E), what do the vertices V and edges E represent?

options.text: V represents IP addresses, E represents MAC addresses
V represents network nodes/routers, E represents physical or logical communication links
V represents application sockets, E represents TCP sequence numbers
V represents autonomous systems, E represents DNS servers

questions.explanation: In network graph theory, vertices represent routing nodes or switches, and edges represent communication links.

questions.question: How does Cisco OSPF calculate the edge weight (cost) of an interface by default?

options.text: Cost = 1 for all interfaces
Cost = Reference Bandwidth (10^8 bps) / Interface Bandwidth (bps)
Cost = Physical Cable Length in meters * 10
Cost = Current packet queue length

questions.explanation: OSPF uses inverse bandwidth: Cost = 100 Mbps / Interface Bandwidth in bps. Higher speed links produce lower costs.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) on an unweighted graph G = (V, E) using an adjacency list?

options.text: O(V + E)
O(E log V)
O(V log V)

questions.explanation: BFS enqueues each vertex at most once and inspects each edge once, yielding O(|V| + |E|) time complexity.

questions.question: Why is standard BFS insufficient for routing in modern heterogeneous networks?

options.text: BFS cannot find cycles in graphs
BFS computes shortest path strictly by hop count, ignoring link capacities, bandwidth, and latency
BFS cannot be implemented with a FIFO queue
BFS requires negative edge weights

questions.explanation: A 1-hop 56 kbps dialup link would be chosen by BFS over a 2-hop 100 Gbps fiber line because BFS treats all link costs as 1.

questions.question: In network topology exploration, how does Depth-First Search (DFS) detect routing loops using the three-color node marking algorithm?

options.text: When an edge points to a BLACK node
When an edge points to a GRAY node (currently on the recursion call stack)
When an edge points to a WHITE node
When all nodes become RED

questions.explanation: A directed edge pointing to a GRAY node represents a back-edge to an active ancestor on the recursion stack, formally proving a cycle.

questions.question: In a network graph, what is an 'articulation point' (cut-vertex)?

options.text: A router whose removal disconnects the remaining network graph into two or more components (Single Point of Failure)
A switch running Spanning Tree Protocol
A port running full-duplex Gigabit Ethernet
A leaf node with degree 1

questions.explanation: An articulation point is a critical network node whose failure partitions the graph, representing a single point of failure (SPOF).

questions.question: What is the foundational prerequisite condition required for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee an optimal shortest path?

options.text: The graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
All edge weights must be strictly non-negative (w >= 0)
The graph must be complete
The number of vertices must equal the number of edges

questions.explanation: Dijkstra relies on the greedy property that extracting the minimum tentative distance node finalizes its optimal distance. This fails if negative weights exist.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with an Adjacency List and a Binary Min-Heap Priority Queue?

options.text: O((V + E) log V)
O(V * E)

questions.explanation: With a binary min-heap: extracting minimums takes O(V log V) and edge relaxations/pushes take O(E log V), totaling O((V + E) log V).

questions.question: In Dijkstra's algorithm, what does the edge relaxation step if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] accomplish?

options.text: It deletes edge (u, v) from the graph
It updates dist[v] to the cheaper path through u and sets predecessor[v] = u
It restarts the priority queue
It switches the network interface to promiscuous mode

questions.explanation: Relaxation tests whether passing through vertex u offers a shorter path to v than previously recorded, updating dist[v] and predecessor pointers.

questions.question: How does a router running OSPF translate Dijkstra's shortest path tree into its physical Forwarding Information Base (FIB)?

options.text: It stores the complete end-to-end path in every packet header
It traces predecessor pointers back from each destination to determine the local outgoing interface and next-hop neighbor IP
It broadcasts the entire tree to the ISP
It copies all routes into the DNS cache

questions.explanation: Hop-by-hop forwarding only requires knowing the immediate Next Hop and physical egress interface for each destination prefix.

questions.question: Which of the following real-world routing protocols utilize Dijkstra's algorithm as their internal path computation engine? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)
RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)

questions.explanation: OSPF and IS-IS are Link-State protocols that execute Dijkstra's algorithm. RIP uses Bellman-Ford, and BGP uses Path Vector.

questions.question: In a 3-node graph with links A-B (cost 4), A-C (cost 2), and C-B (cost 1), what is the shortest path cost from source A to destination B computed by Dijkstra?

options.text: 4 (direct path A-B)
3 (path A-C-B)
5 (path A-B-C)
1 (path C-B)

questions.explanation: A -> C (cost 2) + C -> B (cost 1) = cost 3, which is lower than direct link A -> B (cost 4).

questions.question: What data structure in Dijkstra's algorithm holds the vertices whose shortest path has NOT yet been permanently finalized?

options.text: FIFO Queue
LIFO Stack
Priority Queue (Min-Heap)
Circular Buffer

questions.explanation: A Min-Heap priority queue allows efficient O(log V) extraction of the vertex with the minimum tentative distance.

questions.question: What is the difference between propagation delay and transmission delay when calculating edge weights in a network graph?

options.text: Propagation delay depends on packet length; transmission delay depends on cable length
Propagation delay is the physical time for a signal to travel the cable distance (d / v); transmission delay is the time to push bits onto the wire (L / R)
They are identical terms for latency
Transmission delay occurs only on wireless networks

questions.explanation: Propagation delay = distance / speed of light (approx 200,000 km/s in fiber). Transmission delay = Packet size / Link bandwidth.

questions.question: If an edge weight represents latency, and two paths exist: Path 1 (1 hop, 50ms) and Path 2 (3 hops, 15ms total), which path will Dijkstra choose?

options.text: Path 1, because it has fewer hops
Path 2, because its cumulative edge weight (15ms) is lower
It will randomly alternate between both
It will fail because Path 2 has 3 hops

questions.explanation: Dijkstra minimizes the sum of edge weights along the path, selecting Path 2 (15ms) over Path 1 (50ms).

questions.question: What is asymmetric routing in real-world computer networks?

options.text: Packets from A to B travel via a different physical path than returning packets from B to A
Packets travel faster than the speed of light
A router uses IPv4 for outgoing and IPv6 for incoming packets
Half-duplex Ethernet communication

questions.explanation: Asymmetric routing occurs when outbound and inbound traffic take different network paths due to differing ISP policies or hot-potato routing.

questions.question: In a graph with |V| = 1000 routers and |E| = 3000 links, why is Dijkstra with a binary heap much faster than naive Dijkstra with an array?

options.text: Binary heap runs in O(V + E log V) ≈ 3.3x10^4 ops vs. array O(V^2) = 1,000,000 ops
Binary heap requires no memory
Array implementation cannot handle positive numbers
Binary heap converts graphs into trees

questions.explanation: For sparse graphs (E << V^2), a min-heap scales with O(E log V), which is orders of magnitude faster than searching an array in O(V^2).

questions.question: Can Dijkstra's algorithm detect if a destination node is completely unreachable from the source?

options.text: No, it enters an infinite loop
Yes, unreachable nodes retain their initial tentative distance of infinity (float('inf'))
No, it returns cost 0 for unreachable nodes
It raises a Segmentation Fault

questions.explanation: Vertices in disconnected components are never extracted or relaxed; their recorded distance remains infinity.

questions.question: Which of the following metrics can be legally used as edge weights in Dijkstra's algorithm? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Propagation delay in milliseconds (non-negative)
Hop count (w = 1 for each link)
Financial transit cost in dollars per gigabyte (non-negative)
Negative packet rebate incentives (w < 0)

questions.explanation: Any non-negative cost metric is valid for Dijkstra. Negative metrics (D) violate Dijkstra's greedy invariant and cause incorrect results.

questions.question: How does an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller use graph algorithms compared to traditional distributed routers?

options.text: The centralized SDN controller maintains a global view of all switches and computes optimal paths centrally, downloading flow rules to switches
SDN controllers disable all graph algorithms
SDN switches run Dijkstra independently on each port
SDN switches only support BFS

questions.explanation: In SDN, the control plane is centralized. The SDN controller computes shortest paths globally and installs flow forwarding entries directly into switch TCAMs via OpenFlow.

lecture-06.title: Graph Algorithms for Networking II Quiz
lecture-06.description: 20 questions covering Bellman-Ford, negative weights, Minimum Spanning Trees (Kruskal/Prim), and Spanning Tree Protocol (STP).

questions.question: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail to produce optimal paths when a graph contains negative edge weights?

options.text: Because priority queues cannot store negative numbers
Because its greedy invariant assumes once a node is finalized, its shortest distance cannot be improved by any unexplored path
Because negative numbers cause integer overflow in 32-bit CPUs
Because negative weights turn undirected graphs into directed graphs

questions.explanation: Dijkstra greedily marks the minimum tentative node as permanently optimal. If a negative edge appears later on an alternate path, it could reduce the total cost of an already-finalized node, violating the greedy invariant.

questions.question: What occurs when a directed graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source?

options.text: The shortest path distance between nodes becomes mathematically undefined (-infinity)
The graph automatically converts into a tree
The cycle acts as an infinite bandwidth buffer
The shortest path becomes 0

questions.explanation: Traversing a negative cycle repeatedly reduces the total path cost on each revolution, allowing path cost to decrease indefinitely towards -infinity.

questions.question: In the Bellman-Ford algorithm, why are all edges relaxed exactly |V| - 1 times?

options.text: Because CPU clock cycles are limited to |V| - 1
Because any simple shortest path without cycles in a graph of |V| vertices contains at most |V| - 1 edges
To prevent memory leaks
Because of Ethernet frame padding rules

questions.explanation: A simple path touching |V| vertices has at most |V| - 1 edges. Each relaxation pass guarantees discovery of shortest paths with one additional edge.

questions.question: How does the Bellman-Ford algorithm detect the presence of a reachable negative-weight cycle?

options.text: By checking if the source distance becomes negative
By performing a |V|-th relaxation pass; if any distance dist[v] can still be decreased, a negative cycle exists
By running BFS on the graph
By checking if the priority queue is empty

questions.explanation: If all simple shortest paths are found after |V|-1 passes, a further relaxation on the |V|-th pass can only occur if a negative cycle continues to decrease path costs.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm on a graph with |V| vertices and |E| edges?

options.text: O(V + E)
O(V * E)
O(E log V)

questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford runs |V| - 1 passes, relaxing all |E| edges in each pass, yielding O(|V| * |E|) time complexity.

questions.question: What fundamental routing protocol equation is derived directly from the distributed Bellman-Ford algorithm?

options.text: D_x(y) = min_v { c(x, v) + D_v(y) }
Cost = 10^8 / Bandwidth
MTU = MSS + 40
2^N - 2 >= Hosts

questions.explanation: The Distributed Bellman-Ford equation states that router x reaches destination y with minimum cost by choosing the neighbor v that minimizes the sum of local link cost c(x,v) and v's advertised distance D_v(y).

questions.question: What is the definition of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)?

options.text: A tree connecting all |V| vertices using exactly |V| - 1 edges with the minimum possible total edge weight sum
A tree where every node has degree 2
A directed graph with no negative weights
The shortest path tree from a single root node

questions.explanation: An MST connects all nodes in an undirected graph without cycles (using |V|-1 edges) such that the total sum of edge weights is minimized.

questions.question: How does Kruskal's algorithm construct a Minimum Spanning Tree?

options.text: It explores nodes level-by-level using a FIFO queue
It sorts all edges by weight and greedily adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle using Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
It repeatedly relaxes all edges |V| - 1 times
It begins at a random root and grows outward

questions.explanation: Kruskal's is an edge-centric greedy algorithm: edges are sorted in ascending order and added to the forest if their endpoints belong to different disjoint sets.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Kruskal's algorithm with Disjoint Set Union (path compression and union by rank)?

options.text: O(E log E) = O(E log V)
O(V * E)

questions.explanation: Sorting |E| edges dominates the time complexity, requiring O(|E| log |E|) = O(|E| log |V|). DSU operations run in near-linear O(E α(V)) time.

questions.question: How does Prim's algorithm differ conceptually from Kruskal's algorithm?

options.text: Prim's grows a single connected tree vertex by vertex from an initial root, whereas Kruskal's maintains a forest of disconnected components
Prim's only works on directed graphs
Prim's uses Bellman-Ford internally
Prim's requires negative edge weights

questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm is vertex-centric: it grows a continuous tree by greedily adding the cheapest cut-crossing edge connected to the existing tree.

questions.question: Why are physical loops in Layer 2 switched Ethernet networks catastrophic if Spanning Tree Protocol is disabled?

options.text: Because Ethernet frames lack a Time To Live (TTL) field, causing frames to circulate infinitely and trigger broadcast storms
Because copper wires melt under high voltage
Because IP addresses are automatically deleted
Because DHCP servers stop working

questions.explanation: Unlike Layer 3 IP packets (which are dropped when TTL reaches 0), Layer 2 Ethernet frames have NO TTL field! A looped broadcast circulates forever, crashing the switches.

questions.question: What is MAC table flapping (thrashing) caused by a Layer 2 loop?

options.text: A physical connector becoming loose
A switch repeatedly overwriting the learned port for a MAC address as duplicate looping frames arrive alternately on different ports
A network card alternating between 10 Mbps and 100 Mbps
A DNS server failing to resolve a domain

questions.explanation: Switches learn MAC locations from the source MAC of incoming frames. When duplicate looping frames hit Port 1 then Port 2, the switch MAC table thrashes constantly, exhausting CPU.

questions.question: In the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D), what message unit do switches exchange every 2 seconds to elect the Root Bridge and detect loops?

options.text: ICMP Echo Requests
Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs)
OSPF Hello Packets
ARP Announcements

questions.explanation: Switches exchange Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs) to negotiate the spanning tree topology.

questions.question: How is the STP Root Bridge elected among competing switches in a LAN?

options.text: The switch with the highest IP address wins
The switch with the lowest Bridge ID (Priority + MAC address) wins
The switch connected to the ISP router wins automatically
The switch with the greatest number of physical ports wins

questions.explanation: The switch with the lowest Bridge ID (BID = Priority + MAC) is elected Root Bridge. Default priority is 32768, so lowest MAC breaks ties.

questions.question: What is a 'Root Port' (RP) on a non-root switch in STP?

options.text: The port that connects directly to end-user PCs
The single port on the switch with the lowest cumulative path cost to the Root Bridge
A port that is disabled by the network administrator
A port running optical fiber

questions.explanation: Every non-root switch elects exactly one Root Port: the port offering the lowest total path cost back to the Root Bridge.

questions.question: What happens to a switch port assigned the 'Blocking' (or Alternate) state in STP?

options.text: It turns off electrical power to the port
It drops all user data frames but continues to listen to BPDUs to detect network link failures
It forwards only multicast packets
It acts as a DHCP server

questions.explanation: Blocking ports do not forward user data (breaking the loop), but listen for BPDUs so they can transition to forwarding if a primary link fails.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid STP port transition states in IEEE 802.1D before a port reaches the active Forwarding state? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Blocking
Listening
Learning
Snooping

questions.explanation: Legacy 802.1D transitions through: Blocking -> Listening (15s) -> Learning (15s) -> Forwarding, totaling 30-50s convergence time.

questions.question: Under what condition is the Minimum Spanning Tree of a graph guaranteed to be strictly unique?

options.text: When the graph is bipartite
When all edge weights in the graph are distinct (unique)
When the graph has an odd number of vertices
When all edge weights are negative

questions.explanation: If all edge weights in a connected graph are strictly distinct, the MST is mathematically unique.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Shortest Path Tree (SPT) computed by Dijkstra and a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)?

options.text: An SPT minimizes the distance from one source to all nodes; an MST minimizes the total weight of all edges across the whole graph
An SPT has cycles, while an MST does not
Dijkstra only works on unweighted graphs
An MST requires a designated source root node

questions.explanation: Dijkstra optimizes point-to-point distances from a specific source. MST optimizes total global infrastructure/wire cost.

questions.question: Switch A has MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E and priority 32768. Switch B has MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5F and priority 4096. Which switch becomes the STP Root Bridge?

options.text: Switch A, because its MAC address is numerically smaller
Switch B, because its Bridge Priority (4096) is lower than 32768
Both switches share the Root Bridge duty
Neither, the network will crash

questions.explanation: Bridge ID evaluates Bridge Priority first. Switch B has priority 4096 < 32768, so Switch B wins immediately; MAC addresses are only checked if priorities tie.

lecture-07.title: Routing & Forwarding I Quiz
lecture-07.description: 20 questions covering Control vs Data plane, RIB vs FIB, Longest Prefix Match (LPM), TCAM, and router forwarding lifecycle.

questions.question: What is the fundamental distinction between Routing and Forwarding in computer networks?

options.text: Routing is fast in hardware; Forwarding is slow in software
Routing (Control Plane) determines the end-to-end path; Forwarding (Data Plane) moves packets from input to output interfaces at wire speed
Routing operates at Layer 2; Forwarding operates at Layer 4
Routing is only used on home Wi-Fi routers

questions.explanation: Routing (Control Plane) runs distributed routing protocols on general CPUs to build the map. Forwarding (Data Plane) executes table lookups per packet in hardware ASICs.

questions.question: What is the difference between the RIB (Routing Information Base) and the FIB (Forwarding Information Base)?

options.text: RIB contains all learned candidate routes in CPU RAM; FIB is the compiled, flattened single-best-path table installed in line card silicon memory
RIB stores MAC addresses; FIB stores IP addresses
RIB is located on the user PC; FIB is located in the cloud
They are identical tables with different names

questions.explanation: The RIB holds all candidate routes from OSPF, BGP, static configs. The router compiles the best winning next-hop per prefix into the FIB for nanosecond ASIC lookups.

questions.question: What is the Longest Prefix Match (LPM) rule in IP forwarding?

options.text: The router always selects the route with the lowest metric
When a destination IP matches multiple routing table entries, the router ALWAYS selects the entry with the longest prefix length (most specific mask)
The router forwards to the route learned from the oldest protocol
The router selects the default route 0.0.0.0/0 first

questions.explanation: LPM dictates that the entry matching the greatest number of contiguous network bits (most specific destination range) is selected, overriding metric and administrative distance.

questions.question:
Consider the routing table from the lecture notes:
- 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
- 10.10.0.0/16 via 192.168.2.1 dev eth1
- 10.10.20.0/24 via 192.168.3.1 dev eth2
- 10.10.20.128/25 via 192.168.4.1 dev eth3
- 0.0.0.0/0 via 192.168.5.1 dev eth4

A packet arrives destined for 10.10.20.150. Which interface will the router forward it to?
questions.explanation: 10.10.20.150 matches /8, /16, /24, and /25. By Longest Prefix Match, /25 (25 bits) is the longest and most specific prefix. The router forwards out eth3.

questions.question: Using the same table from question 4, where is a packet destined for 10.10.20.50 forwarded?
questions.explanation: 10.10.20.50 falls into .0-.127, so it does NOT match /25 (.128-.255). Among the remaining matching entries (/8, /16, /24), /24 is the longest match (eth2).

questions.question: Using the same table from question 4, where is a packet destined for 8.8.8.8 forwarded?

options.text: eth0
eth1
eth4 (0.0.0.0/0 Default Route)
The packet is dropped immediately

questions.explanation: 8.8.8.8 does not match 10.x.x.x. It matches only the default route 0.0.0.0/0, forwarding out eth4 to 192.168.5.1.

questions.question: What is the Linux command to manually add a static route for network 172.16.1.0/24 via gateway 10.0.0.2 out interface eth1 (as highlighted in the handwritten notes)?

options.text: ip route add 172.16.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.2 dev eth1
ifconfig eth1 172.16.1.0 netmask 10.0.0.2
netstat add 172.16.1.0 via eth1

questions.explanation: The modern Linux iproute2 syntax is: 'ip route add <prefix> via <gateway> dev <interface>'.

questions.question: Which Linux command manually inserts a static neighbor MAC address entry into the ARP cache table (from the handwritten notes)?

options.text: arp -s 10.0.0.2 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
sudo ip neigh add 10.0.0.2 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff dev eth1
ip link set 10.0.0.2 address aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
route add -host 10.0.0.2 lladdr aa:bb

questions.explanation: 'sudo ip neigh add <ip> lladdr <mac> dev <interface>' is the canonical iproute2 command for static neighbor table management.

questions.question: According to standard Unix/Linux networking conventions (referenced in the handwritten notes), what do the interface names 'lo', 'eth0', and 'wlan0' signify? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: lo represents the software Loopback interface
eth0 represents the first wired physical Ethernet interface
wlan0 represents the first Wireless Local Area Network (Wi-Fi) interface
eth0 is reserved strictly for default gateway routers

questions.explanation: lo = loopback (127.0.0.1), eth0 = first Ethernet NIC, wlan0 = first Wi-Fi adapter.

questions.question: Why is a /30 subnet typically configured on router WAN interfaces connected to an ISP (e.g. eth1 10.0.0.1/30)?

options.text: Because ISPs only support 30 Mbps bandwidth
Because a /30 provides exactly 2 usable host IPs (one for the customer router, one for the ISP gateway) with zero wasted address space
Because it disables ARP
Because 30 is a prime number

questions.explanation: A /30 contains 4 IP addresses (2^2): 1 network, 2 usable hosts, 1 broadcast. Perfect for point-to-point router links without wasting public IPs.

questions.question: What is the third bit state supported by TCAM (Ternary Content Addressable Memory) in router silicon, beyond binary 0 and 1?

options.text: Error (E)
Don't Care / Wildcard (X)
High Voltage (H)
Float (F)

questions.explanation: TCAM supports 0, 1, and X (Don't Care / Masked bits), enabling single-clock-cycle parallel Longest Prefix Match lookups across 1,000,000 entries.

questions.question: What is the lookup time complexity of a hardware TCAM in an enterprise router line card?

options.text: O(1) — constant time in a single hardware clock cycle
O(N) — linear scan of all routes
O(log N)

questions.explanation: TCAM circuits compare the incoming destination IP against all routing entries in parallel in a single hardware cycle (typically 2-5 nanoseconds).

questions.question: What data structure is commonly used in software routing engines (like the Linux kernel FIB) to perform Longest Prefix Match lookups efficiently?

options.text: Linked List
Patricia / Radix Trie (bit-compressed prefix tree)
Circular Ring Buffer
Binary Search Tree on destination IP

questions.explanation: A Radix/Patricia Trie branches on bits (0 = left, 1 = right) with path compression, finding the longest matching prefix in at most 32 bit steps (O(32) = O(1)).

questions.question: What happens in Step 4 of the router packet forwarding lifecycle when the IPv4 TTL field is decremented to 0?

options.text: The router resets TTL to 64 and forwards the packet
The router drops the packet and transmits an ICMP Type 11 (Time-to-Live Exceeded in Transit) message back to the source
The router saves the packet to hard disk
The router broadcasts the packet to all ports

questions.explanation: TTL decrementing kills looping packets. When TTL reaches 0, the packet is discarded and an ICMP Type 11 Code 0 is returned to the source.

questions.question: Why MUST a router recalculate the IPv4 Header Checksum at every single forwarding hop?

options.text: Because the source MAC address changes
Because the TTL field was decremented by 1, changing the arithmetic sum of the header bits
Because the TCP payload changes
Because the router clock is synchronized with NTP

questions.explanation: The IPv4 checksum covers the entire IP header. Because TTL decreases by 1, the checksum is invalid and must be updated.

questions.question: What is a 'Floating Static Route'?

options.text: A route configured without an IP address
A backup static route configured with a higher Administrative Distance that only becomes active if the primary dynamic/static route fails
A route used on cruise ships
A route that moves across interfaces automatically

questions.explanation: By setting an AD higher than the primary link (e.g. AD 10 vs primary AD 1), the floating static route stays dormant until the primary link drops, achieving automatic failover.

questions.question: In Cisco IOS routing tables, what does the notation [110/20] beside an OSPF route indicate?

options.text: 110 seconds remaining before timeout; 20 hops
Administrative Distance = 110 (trustworthiness); Metric/Cost = 20
110 packets forwarded; 20 packets dropped
Port 110 mapped to Port 20

questions.explanation: The first number is Administrative Distance (AD), where lower AD is preferred between protocols. The second number is the internal metric/cost.

questions.question: Which of the following actions occur during Step 9 of the router forwarding lifecycle when transmitting a packet onto the egress wire? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: The router sets the destination MAC to the Next-Hop router's MAC address
The router sets the source MAC to its own outgoing interface MAC address
The router recalculates the Layer 2 CRC-32 Frame Check Sequence (FCS)
The router modifies the destination IP address to match the next hop

questions.explanation: A, B, and C describe Layer 2 encapsulation. D is incorrect: destination IP is never modified by standard routers (only by NAT).

questions.question: How does the diagnostic utility 'traceroute' exploit router forwarding behavior to discover each hop along an internet path?

options.text: It asks the DNS root server for the list of routers
It sends sequential packets starting with TTL=1, TTL=2, TTL=3..., eliciting ICMP Time Exceeded responses from each intermediate router
It inspects the BGP table on the client computer
It forces routers to broadcast their MAC addresses

questions.explanation: Traceroute sends packets with incremental TTLs. The 1st router drops TTL=1 and replies with ICMP Time Exceeded; the 2nd router drops TTL=2, revealing their IP addresses hop-by-hop.

questions.question: If two adjacent routers mistakenly configure static routes pointing to each other for the same destination subnet, what happens to packets sent to that subnet?

options.text: They bounce back and forth between the two routers until their TTL reaches 0 and they are dropped
They are automatically forwarded to Google DNS
They are absorbed by the ARP cache
The routers crash immediately

questions.explanation: This creates a routing loop. Packets bounce between the two routers on the physical link, decrementing TTL by 1 per hop until TTL=0, where they are discarded.

lecture-08.title: Routing & Forwarding II Quiz
lecture-08.description: 20 questions covering Distance Vector (RIP), Count-to-Infinity, Split Horizon, Link-State (OSPF), Areas, and BGP Path Vector.

questions.question: Why is Distance Vector routing often characterized as 'Routing by Rumor'?

options.text: Because routers broadcast news headlines
Because routers do not know the global network topology; they blindly accept distance claims advertised by immediate neighbors
Because distance vector protocols use unencrypted UDP packets
Because it relies on social network graphs

questions.explanation: Routers in Distance Vector share their whole table with neighbors. A router trusts its neighbor's reported distance without independently verifying the actual path.

questions.question: In RIP (Routing Information Protocol), what is the maximum valid hop count metric, and what value represents 'Infinity' (unreachable)?

options.text: Max metric is 15; 16 represents Infinity
Max metric is 255; 256 represents Infinity
Max metric is 100; 101 represents Infinity
Max metric is 7; 8 represents Infinity

questions.explanation: RIP caps networks at 15 hops to mitigate count-to-infinity delays. Metric 16 is defined as unreachable (Infinity).

questions.question: How frequently does a standard RIPv2 router broadcast/multicast its entire routing table to its neighbors?

options.text: Every 5 seconds
Every 30 seconds
Every 5 minutes
Only when an administrator types a command

questions.explanation: RIP sends unsolicited periodic full-table updates every 30 seconds via UDP port 520 (multicast 224.0.0.9 in RIPv2).

questions.question: What causes the 'Count-to-Infinity' problem in Distance Vector routing?

options.text: Routers running out of memory
When a destination link fails, neighbors mutually believe the other still has a path, slowly incrementing the hop count between themselves until reaching 16
BGP peering sessions timing out
Broadcast storms on Ethernet switches

questions.explanation: Router B advertises a path that depended on C. When C's link drops, C assumes B has an alternate route and updates its cost. B then updates its cost from C, ping-ponging to 16.

questions.question: What is the core operational rule of the 'Split Horizon' loop prevention mechanism?

options.text: Split routing tables into two halves
Never advertise a route back out the same interface through which it was originally learned
Disable all default routes
Send updates only during nighttime

questions.explanation: Split Horizon prevents loops by forbidding a router from advertising a route back to the neighbor that taught it that route in the first place.

questions.question: How does 'Poison Reverse' modify the standard Split Horizon rule?

options.text: It sends corrupt checksums
Instead of suppressing the advertisement, it explicitly advertises the route back to the source with metric = 16 (Infinity / Poisoned)
It resets the interface MTU to 0
It floods ICMP redirects

questions.explanation: Poison Reverse actively advertises unreachable (hop 16) back out the ingress interface, eliminating race conditions in multi-router topologies.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'Hold-Down Timer' in distance vector routing?

options.text: To pause packet transmission when CPU temperature rises
When a route is marked down, the router ignores any new updates for that route for a stabilization window (e.g. 180s) to allow loop flushes
To keep the interface link up during cable unplugging
To synchronize router clocks with UTC

questions.explanation: Hold-down timers prevent premature acceptance of stale or looping route claims while the network topology is still stabilizing.

questions.question: What is a 'Triggered Update' (Flash Update) in distance vector protocols?

options.text: An update sent immediately when a route metric changes, without waiting for the 30-second timer to expire
An update triggered by an email alert
An update containing security patches
A packet sent to wake up sleeping routers

questions.explanation: Triggered updates accelerate convergence by broadcasting link failures the exact microsecond they occur.

questions.question: How does Link-State routing (OSPF) fundamentally differ from Distance Vector routing?

options.text: Link-state routers exchange entire routing tables; distance vector routers exchange single packets
Every link-state router floods local Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) so all routers build an identical Link-State Database (LSDB), then run Dijkstra independently
Link-state protocols only work on Wi-Fi
Distance vector uses Dijkstra; link-state uses Bellman-Ford

questions.explanation: Link-state routers have complete visibility of the entire topological map (LSDB) and independently compute their own shortest-path tree using Dijkstra.

questions.question: Which of the following are standard OSPF packet types? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Hello Packet (Type 1)
Database Description / DBD (Type 2)
Link State Request / LSR (Type 3)
Link State Update / LSU (Type 4)

questions.explanation: OSPF defines 5 packet types: Hello, DBD, LSR, LSU, and LSAck (Type 5).

questions.question: What transport layer protocol does OSPF use to carry its control packets across intermediate links?

options.text: TCP Port 179
UDP Port 520
Raw IP directly using Protocol Number 89
HTTP/2

questions.explanation: OSPF does not use TCP or UDP. It encapsulates packets directly in raw IPv4/IPv6 packets with IP Protocol Number 89.

questions.question: What is the mandatory central area in a hierarchical OSPF deployment to which all other areas must connect?

options.text: Area 1 (Stub Area)
Area 0 (Backbone Area)
Area 255 (Transit Area)
Area 100 (Autonomous Area)

questions.explanation: Area 0 (0.0.0.0) is the core Backbone Area. All inter-area traffic must transit through Area 0 to prevent routing loops.

questions.question: What is the role of an Area Border Router (ABR) in OSPF?

options.text: A router that connects to external non-OSPF networks like BGP
A router with interfaces in Area 0 and one or more standard areas, summarizing routes and confining SPF recalculations
A router that operates as a DNS caching resolver
A router that only forwards multicast traffic

questions.explanation: ABRs connect Area 0 to sub-areas. They summarize internal area topology into summary LSAs, preventing link flaps in one area from triggering SPF runs in other areas.

questions.question: On a broadcast multi-access Ethernet network with N = 10 OSPF routers, how many adjacencies would form without DR/BDR election?
questions.explanation: Full mesh peering requires N(N-1)/2 adjacencies. For 10 routers, that is 10*9/2 = 45 redundant adjacencies flooding duplicate LSAs.

questions.question: How does the election of a Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) solve this scalability bottleneck?

options.text: It turns off 8 of the 10 routers
Routers form adjacencies ONLY with the DR and BDR (multicast 224.0.0.6), reducing adjacencies from O(N^2) to O(N)
It switches from OSPF to RIP
It enables full-duplex transmission

questions.explanation: All other routers (DROthers) peer only with the DR/BDR, reducing total adjacencies to 2N - 3, dramatically conserving CPU and link bandwidth.

questions.question: What is an Autonomous System (AS) in the context of global internet routing?

options.text: A self-driving automobile network
A collection of connected IP routing networks controlled by a single administrative entity with a unified routing policy (e.g. AS15169 for Google)
A single home Wi-Fi router
An artificial intelligence model that manages routers

questions.explanation: An Autonomous System (AS) is an administrative domain (e.g. ISP, university, tech giant) identified by a globally unique Autonomous System Number (ASN).

questions.question: What protocol is the de facto standard Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) routing the global internet between different Autonomous Systems?

options.text: RIPv2
OSPFv3
BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol Version 4)
IS-IS

questions.explanation: BGP-4 is the glue of the internet, exchanging reachability and policy paths between thousands of global Autonomous Systems.

questions.question: Why is BGP classified as a 'Path Vector' protocol rather than pure Distance Vector or Link State?

options.text: Because it routes vectors of floating point numbers
Because it advertises the complete sequence of Autonomous System Numbers (AS_PATH) traversed to reach each destination prefix
Because it uses vector graphics for network maps
Because it runs over UDP

questions.explanation: Instead of advertising pure hop counts, BGP includes the entire path of ASNs in the AS_PATH attribute.

questions.question: How does BGP's AS_PATH attribute provide immediate, foolproof routing loop detection without running Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.text: If a border router receives a BGP advertisement containing its own Autonomous System Number in the AS_PATH, it immediately discards the route
It checks if the AS_PATH has more than 16 hops
It pings all ASNs in the path
It computes a CRC-32 on the ASNs

questions.explanation: If a router sees its own ASN in the AS_PATH, it knows the route has already passed through its network, so accepting it would create an inter-domain loop. It drops it instantly.

questions.question: What transport layer protocol and port number does BGP use to establish reliable peer sessions?

options.text: UDP Port 520
Raw IP Protocol 89
TCP Port 179
TLS Port 443

questions.explanation: BGP relies on TCP Port 179 for point-to-point connection establishment, retransmission, and reliability.

lecture-09.title: DNS & Internet Applications Quiz
lecture-09.description: 20 questions covering DNS hierarchy, query resolution, record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, PTR), URL parsing, HTTP protocol, status codes, and cookies.

questions.question: What is the primary motivation for using the Domain Name System (DNS) instead of relying directly on hardcoded IP addresses?

options.text: DNS encrypts all web traffic by default using TLS
Domain names decouple service identity from volatile physical IP addresses, enabling load balancing and seamless IP renumbering
IP addresses cannot be routed across continental fiber lines
Domain names eliminate the need for Layer 3 IP routing

questions.explanation: DNS decouples human-readable identifiers from underlying numeric IP addresses. This allows servers to migrate IPs, distribute traffic across geo-distributed servers (CDNs), and provide failover without breaking bookmarks or client code.

questions.question: In the hierarchical DNS tree structure, which tier is responsible for knowing the authoritative nameservers of Top-Level Domains like .com, .org, and .edu?

options.text: Authoritative Nameservers
Root Nameservers (represented by the trailing dot '.')
Local Recursive Resolvers
Client OS Stub Resolvers

questions.explanation: The Root Nameservers sit at the apex of the DNS hierarchy (denoted by the invisible trailing dot in fully qualified domain names like `example.com.`). They maintain delegations to the TLD nameservers.

questions.question: How are the 13 logical root server IP addresses (a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net) scaled globally to handle billions of queries without collapsing?

options.text: Using BGP Anycast routing to broadcast the same 13 IP addresses from hundreds of physical data centers worldwide
By storing all internet domain records on a single quantum supercomputer in Virginia
By forcing client web browsers to execute DNS root queries locally
By assigning each root server a unique 64-bit IPv8 address

questions.explanation: Through BGP Anycast, the same 13 logical IP addresses are announced by over 1,500 physical server instances distributed across the globe. Border routers direct DNS queries to the topologically nearest physical instance.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a 'Recursive Query' and an 'Iterative Query' in DNS resolution?

options.text: Recursive queries use TCP; iterative queries use UDP
In a recursive query, the contacted server assumes responsibility to find the final answer; in an iterative query, the server returns the best referral (next nameserver) it knows
Recursive queries only resolve IPv6 addresses; iterative queries resolve IPv4
Iterative queries repeat infinitely until the client manually interrupts them

questions.explanation: A recursive query asks the resolver: 'Please do whatever work is necessary to bring me the final IP.' An iterative query asks: 'If you don't know the exact answer, give me the IP of the next nameserver down the tree who might know.'

questions.question: Which DNS record type maps an IPv6 host address to a domain name?

options.text: A record
AAAA record (Quad-A)
CNAME record
PTR record

questions.explanation: An 'A' record maps a hostname to a 32-bit IPv4 address, whereas a 'AAAA' (Quad-A) record maps a hostname to a 128-bit IPv6 address.

questions.question: Why is it forbidden by RFC standards to define a CNAME record at the root apex of a domain (e.g. at 'example.com' without a subdomain prefix)?

options.text: Because CNAME records cannot coexist with other essential record types like SOA and NS at the zone apex
Because CNAME records exceed 1500 bytes
Because CNAME records can only point to numeric IP addresses
Because root apex names can only contain letters, not dots

questions.explanation: RFC 1034 states that if a CNAME record exists for a node, no other data records can exist for that node. Because a zone apex MUST contain SOA and NS records, a CNAME cannot be placed at the naked apex domain.

questions.question: Which DNS record type is specifically used by mail transfer agents (MTAs) to route emails to the destination organization's mail servers?

options.text: TXT record
MX record
PTR record
SRV record

questions.explanation: MX (Mail Exchanger) records specify the mail servers responsible for accepting emails for a domain, along with priority values for failover.

questions.question: For what security and verification purposes are DNS TXT records widely utilized in modern cloud infrastructure? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) to prevent email spoofing
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) public cryptographic key publication
Domain ownership verification for SSL/TLS certificates and Google Search Console
Translating MAC addresses into IPv4 addresses

questions.explanation: TXT records hold arbitrary text attributes, commonly used for email validation (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and verifying administrative domain ownership. Translating MAC to IP is handled by ARP/RARP, not DNS TXT.

questions.question: What is the function of the TTL (Time to Live) field returned in a DNS resource record?

options.text: It specifies the number of router hops the packet can survive before being dropped
It dictates the number of seconds intermediate recursive resolvers and clients may cache the record before querying authoritative servers again
It defines the server's session timeout in minutes
It specifies the lifespan of the domain registration at the registrar

questions.explanation: DNS TTL tells caching resolvers how long (in seconds) the answer remains fresh. A lower TTL allows faster propagation of IP changes during migrations, while a higher TTL reduces DNS query traffic.

questions.question: In the URL `https://api.scaler.com:8443/v1/students?sort=desc#results`, what constitutes the 'query string' component?

options.text: api.scaler.com
sort=desc
#results

questions.explanation: The URL anatomy is: scheme (`https`), host (`api.scaler.com`), port (`8443`), path (`/v1/students`), query string (`sort=desc`, starting after `?`), and fragment identifier (`results`, starting after `#`).

questions.question: Why is the fragment identifier (e.g. `#section2` in `https://example.com/docs#section2`) NEVER transmitted over the wire to the web server in an HTTP GET request?

options.text: Because HTTP headers cannot contain the '#' character
Because fragments are strictly client-side browser instructions to scroll to or anchor on a specific element after parsing the HTML
Because TLS encryption strips fragment identifiers for security reasons
Because routers drop packets with hashtag symbols

questions.explanation: Fragment identifiers designate internal anchors within a resource. The web browser processes them locally after receiving the full document; hence, the browser omits the fragment when making the HTTP request.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between an HTTP method being 'Safe' versus being 'Idempotent'?

options.text: Safe methods use HTTPS; idempotent methods use HTTP
Safe methods do not alter server state (read-only); Idempotent methods can alter state, but executing them multiple times produces the identical side-effect as executing them once
Idempotent methods are read-only; safe methods can delete records
Safe methods run in O(1) time; idempotent methods run in O(N) time

questions.explanation: Safe methods (like GET, HEAD) do not mutate resource state. Idempotent methods (like PUT, DELETE, GET) can modify state, but repeating identical requests N times leaves the server in the exact same state as 1 request.

questions.question: Which of the following HTTP methods are classified as Idempotent according to RFC 9110? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: GET
PUT
DELETE
POST

questions.explanation: GET (safe and idempotent), PUT (replacing a resource repeatedly yields the same resource state), and DELETE (deleting resource X repeatedly leaves it deleted) are idempotent. POST is typically NOT idempotent (e.g. creating new orders).

questions.question: What is the key difference between HTTP PUT and HTTP PATCH?

options.text: PUT is for web pages; PATCH is for mobile apps
PUT replaces the entire target resource with the uploaded payload; PATCH applies partial modifications/deltas to the existing resource
PUT is non-idempotent; PATCH is strictly idempotent
PUT requires authentication; PATCH is anonymous

questions.explanation: PUT represents a full replacement: any omitted fields are typically cleared or set to defaults. PATCH provides instructions to partially mutate only specific fields without modifying the rest.

questions.question: What does an HTTP 301 Moved Permanently status code instruct a web browser and search engine crawler to do differently compared to a 302 Found?

options.text: 301 instructs clients and search engines to permanently cache the redirect and update links/SEO rankings to the new URI; 302 is temporary and should not be cached permanently
301 means the page has an error; 302 means the page is successful
301 disables TLS encryption on the new location
301 requires entering a new username and password

questions.explanation: 301 signifies permanent relocation; browsers cache it aggressively and search engines transfer page rank to the new URL. 302 is a temporary redirection, so search engines keep indexing the original URL.

questions.question: What is the architectural difference between an HTTP 401 Unauthorized and an HTTP 403 Forbidden status code?

options.text: 401 means the client must provide authentication credentials (unauthenticated); 403 means the identity is known but the user lacks permission to access the resource (unauthorized)
401 is a server error; 403 is a client error
401 is returned only over HTTP; 403 is returned only over HTTPS
401 indicates that the server's database is offline

questions.explanation: 401 implies 'who are you? Please log in.' 403 implies 'I know who you are, but you do not have permission to touch this resource.'

questions.question: What is the critical security vulnerability prevented by setting the 'HttpOnly' flag on a Set-Cookie header?

options.text: Man-in-the-middle sniffing of packets over open Wi-Fi
Session hijacking via Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) where malicious JavaScript accesses `document.cookie`
SQL Injection attacks on the backend database
Denial of Service attacks against the web server

questions.explanation: The `HttpOnly` flag prevents client-side scripts (like JavaScript running via XSS) from reading the cookie via `document.cookie`, mitigating cookie theft and session hijacking.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'SameSite=Strict' cookie attribute?

options.text: It forces the cookie to only be transmitted over HTTPS connections
It prevents the browser from sending the cookie on ANY cross-site request (mitigating Cross-Site Request Forgery / CSRF)
It expires the cookie after strictly 5 minutes
It prevents users from logging in on mobile devices

questions.explanation: `SameSite=Strict` guarantees the cookie is never sent in third-party contexts (e.g. following links from external sites or embedded iframes), eliminating CSRF vulnerabilities for authenticated state.

questions.question: In a modern stateless web application using JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for sessions, where is the session state primarily stored?

options.text: In a centralized Redis database on the server
Directly inside the cryptographically signed JWT payload held and presented by the client
In the router's ARP table
In the DNS SOA record

questions.explanation: Stateless JWT tokens encode user identity and claims directly in the token payload, signed by the server's private secret. Any backend server can verify the signature without reading a centralized database.

questions.question: How does DNS-based Round-Robin Load Balancing distribute client requests among multiple backend web servers?

options.text: The authoritative DNS server rotates the ordering of multiple IP addresses in the 'A' record answer set on each query
The client router picks the server with the lowest MAC address
The DNS server opens TCP connections to test each backend server's CPU load
The DNS root servers route packets through a reverse proxy

questions.explanation: In Round-Robin DNS, multiple A records are configured for the same domain. The DNS server permutes the list on successive responses, distributing incoming connections across multiple IP addresses.

lecture-10.title: TCP, UDP & Socket Programming Quiz
lecture-10.description: 20 questions covering transport layer multiplexing, ports, TCP 3-way handshake, 4-way teardown, TIME_WAIT, sliding window, congestion control, and Python socket programming.

questions.question: While the Network Layer (IP) provides host-to-host packet delivery, what essential abstraction does the Transport Layer (Layer 4) provide?

options.text: Hop-by-hop framing across fiber cables
Process-to-process communication using port numbers (demultiplexing)
Global path computation using BGP
Translating domain names into 32-bit integers
